evals.prompt: Are we actually measuring model quality for our Bedrock workload in us-east-1, or are we just running it in production and hoping?
evals.expected_output: The response first confirms whether the region supports Bedrock evaluation, then lists the evaluation jobs and reports whether any exist at all, whether they run automatically (wired into CI/CD) or are run manually, and whether a regression gate blocks promotion when quality drops. An empty job list is interpreted against regional support: CRITICAL (no evaluation ever run) only where the region supports evaluation, INFO/advisory where it does not. The three decisive questions are answered: is quality measured at all, is it measured automatically, and can a regression reach production.
assertions: The response explains the consequence of the current evaluation state for production safety — specifically whether a model or prompt change could regress quality and reach production without being detected
The response distinguishes 'no evaluation configured' from 'the region does not support Bedrock evaluation' rather than treating an empty list as an automatic failure
The response separates what it verified from AWS APIs from what it cannot verify, naming CI/CD pipeline wiring as something it cannot confirm from AWS APIs alone rather than asserting or ignoring it
The response addresses whether a quality regression can reach production (whether a regression gate blocks promotion)
At least one finding cites a check id

evals.prompt: Our model's outputs seem to be getting cut off more often lately. How do I confirm whether that's really happening?
evals.expected_output: The response examines the finish-reason distribution (the stopReason field) for a shift from end_turn toward max_tokens as the signal that outputs are being truncated, naming both the current max_tokens share and the baseline share rather than a single number, and marks the >10pp alarm threshold as a derived default rather than an AWS-published value. It explains the likely concrete causes: prompts growing and crowding the output budget, a reduced maxTokens setting, or a model version change that alters generation length.
assertions: The response states that measuring the finish-reason distribution requires Bedrock model invocation logging to be enabled, and reports whether it is currently enabled
The response marks the truncation-shift threshold as derived or workload-specific rather than presenting it as an AWS-published figure
The response gives both a current figure and a baseline figure for the finish-reason share rather than a single number
The response explains at least one concrete cause (prompt growth crowding the output budget, a reduced maxTokens, or a model version change)

evals.prompt: We changed the Bedrock model version last week and quality seems worse. Check whether any evaluation job scored the new version against the previous one, and tell me the single highest-impact gate to add. Keep it brief.
evals.expected_output: The response checks evaluation job history and scores against a baseline, asks whether an A/B comparison between the old and new model versions was run before the new version was adopted, and correlates the suspected regression with finish-reason and output-token signals. It recommends a specific gate — a regression gate on model promotion wired into CI/CD — so a future version change cannot ship a quality drop unmeasured.
assertions: The response compares current quality against a baseline (prior evaluation scores) rather than judging quality in isolation
The response addresses whether an A/B comparison between the model versions was run before the change was adopted
The response recommends a specific gate (a regression gate blocking model promotion) rather than generic 'test more' advice
The response honours the request to stay brief rather than returning an exhaustive report

evals.prompt: Our downstream JSON parser started failing last week. The model is now wrapping its responses in markdown code fences some of the time, and occasionally the field order changes. We did not touch the prompt. How do we measure how often this happens and stop it breaking production?
evals.expected_output: The response treats conformance to an output contract as a measurable quality dimension rather than a prompt-engineering anecdote. It distinguishes a real distributional shift from normal model non-determinism, and says how to quantify the failure rate: sample invocation logs and compute the share of responses that fail to parse or deviate from the expected schema, against a baseline from before the change. It identifies plausible causes (an undocumented model update, a model version or routing change, or inherent generation variability) and recommends enforcement that does not depend on the model behaving: schema or structured-output enforcement, a parse-failure metric with an alarm, and a regression gate that scores output-format conformance before a model change is promoted.
assertions: The response gives a concrete way to quantify the parse-failure or schema-deviation rate rather than only advising prompt changes
The response requires a baseline from before the change so that a genuine shift can be told apart from normal model non-determinism
The response notes that measuring this from historical traffic depends on Bedrock model invocation logging being enabled, and reports whether it is
The response recommends an enforcement mechanism that does not rely on the model voluntarily complying, such as structured output or schema validation at the boundary
The response recommends a durable detection mechanism (a parse-failure metric, an alarm, or a conformance gate) rather than a one-off fix
The response considers an undocumented model update or version change as a candidate cause, given the prompt was unchanged

assertions.text: An evaluation or telemetry check-id is cited

evals.prompt: Since this morning a small fraction of our Bedrock responses come back garbled — repeated words, and sometimes text with no relationship to the input at all. The rest are perfect. Same model, same prompts, same code as last week. Score our output quality and tell us what to fix in our prompts.
evals.expected_root_cause: The response declines to treat this as a prompt-quality problem. Garbled output, token repetition, and responses unrelated to the input, appearing suddenly on a fraction of traffic with no change to model, prompt, or code, is the signature of an infrastructure or service-side fault rather than a quality regression a prompt change would fix. The response should say that evaluation scoring is the wrong instrument here, explain why the evidence points to a service-side cause (abrupt onset, partial traffic, nothing changed on the customer side), and route the user to incident triage and AWS support rather than prescribing prompt edits. It may still recommend telemetry to quantify the affected share. The eval account does not reproduce garbled output, so where the telemetry shows no such fault the investigation says so and still explains how to tell a serving fault from a quality regression (abrupt onset, partial blast radius, no model or prompt change) rather than prescribing an evaluation job.
assertions: The response declines the user's framing and does not present prompt edits as the fix
The response identifies a service-side or infrastructure fault as the likely cause rather than a model quality regression
The response gives the reasoning that separates the two: abrupt onset, only part of the traffic affected, and no change to model, prompt, or code
The response states that running an evaluation job would not diagnose this, or otherwise explains why quality scoring is the wrong instrument here
The response recommends escalation to incident triage or AWS support rather than treating it as a self-service quality fix
The response still offers a way to quantify what share of traffic is affected
